title: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki calls for 'extreme caution' as scaling outruns alignment
subtitle: In an essay titled 'An Alien Mind,' Pachocki says no frontier lab has solved alignment well enough to keep scaling at full speed — and expects voluntary slowdowns.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published a personal essay on September 7 titled 'An Alien Mind,' arguing that the pace of AI capability gains has outrun the industry's ability to align and monitor the systems being built. 'This is a time that calls for extreme caution,' Pachocki wrote. 'I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence.' The essay was picked up by Bloomberg the same day and reprinted or covered by The Next Web, Business Today, and Insurance Journal on September 7 and 8.

Pachocki's specific claim is unusually direct for a sitting chief scientist at a frontier lab. He states that 'currently I believe that no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer,' and that he 'expects and hopes for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.' He also flags recursive self-improvement — models that meaningfully accelerate their own development — as a near-term rather than distant concern, based on internal OpenAI results.

The essay lands in a specific context. It follows the GPT-6 Astra system card, released September 6, which documented a measurable decline in chain-of-thought monitorability at higher capability tiers, and the DSEwiki agent-hijack incident earlier in the same week. It also follows Sanders and Casar's Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act being introduced on September 5. A chief scientist calling publicly for slowdowns while the lab ships its most capable model to date is either a genuine institutional split going public or a pre-emptive positioning move ahead of Anthropic's October IPO roadshow — either reading matters for how the next six months of AI policy unfold.

For learners: pay attention to who is saying this and what they are not saying. Pachocki does not call for a moratorium, does not name a specific capability threshold, and does not commit OpenAI to a slowdown — he calls for voluntary industry slowdowns 'until shared safety bars are established.' That gap between 'we should slow down' and 'we are slowing down' is where AI governance actually happens. When you read AI-safety statements from lab leaders, always ask what commitment, if any, is being made — and who would enforce it if it were.
